# Ramona

Ramona is a model/generator/validation framework which allows user to generate files form configurations. Utilizes Jinja2 for generation.

Cool image that i generated with AI :)  
<img src="docs/images/scaled.png" width="192" height="220" alt="Ramona logo" style="image-rendering: pixelated;">

## Why Ramona workflow
Ramona puts configuration, generation, and validation in one project workflow:

- Define project and model objects in YAML(for now).
	- Compose configuration with `include` and `extends`.
	- Resolve values and references with project, model, scope, and object context.
- Generate
	- Render Jinja2 templates into SQL, Python, DAGs, or other text files.
	- Copy files or directories into generated output locations.
- Validate:
	- Add Python model checks with the `@modelcheck` decorator.


## Requirements

see [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml)


## Installation

Clone the repository and install Ramona in editable mode:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/ozcanseker/Ramona.git
cd Ramona
python -m pip install -e .
```

To install the development dependency as well:

```powershell
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

This exposes the `ramona` command in the active Python environment.

## Quick Start

Run commands from a directory containing `ramona.yaml`:

```powershell
ramona generate
ramona modelcheck
```

The configuration path defaults to `./ramona.yaml`. Use `-rcp` or
`--ramona-config-path` to select another project:

```powershell
ramona -rcp .\sample_projects\project_for_development\ramona.yaml modelcheck
```

`generate` builds the project and renders or copies its configured outputs.
It cleans the configured generated paths before writing. `modelcheck` builds
the same project and runs all discovered model checks. Both commands write a
log to the project directory at `log/ramona.log`.

## How to Use Ramona

### 1. Project config
Ramona uses a ramona.yaml to define a ramona project config. This have some keywords that are needed to get started:

see [example config](sample_projects\duck_db_dwh\ramona.yaml)

protectsL keywords
MODELS_DIR = Where the models are located  
TEMPLATES_DIR = Where the templates for generation are located  
GENERATED_PATHS = List of outputs for the application, Carefull the app also cleans these locations before generation  
MODELCHECKS = dit where the modelchecks are located

Other than this, you are free to define all the keys you want. These defined keys will be available in downstream models during parsing of yaml and generation,

### 1. Define a Model

Create a model directory below `models_dir` and add a model configuration. A
model can contain shared configuration and one or more objects:

see [example config](sample_projects\duck_db_dwh\ramona.yaml)

```yaml
# models/warehouse/model_config.yaml
id: warehouse
type: table
output_dir: ./sql/warehouse/
template_config:
- template: ./table.sql.jinja2
objects:
- id: customers
	name: customers_current
	columns:
	- id: customer_id
		datatype: INTEGER
	- id: email
		datatype: VARCHAR
```

one model config.yaml is rquired per model. 

The most important thing in the model configs are the objects. These will be the things that will be given to the generator. So scope of project is:
- Projectconfig
- Modelconfig
- Objects

The objects will also get the keys of the model_config. The model_config does not have to contain all the information. you can for example create the following file structure for your model:

- ramona.yaml
- models
	- model_config.yml
	- tables
		- tables_config.yml
		- tables:
			- table_1
			- table_2
	- dags
		- dags_config.yml

the objects in table 1 and 2 will inherit the tables_config.yml, ramona.yaml and model_config.yaml keys, while the dags_config.yaml object will inherit only model_config and ramona_config.yaml.

#### 2.1. Compose Values and References

Use Ramona's context functions when a value depends on another project or
model setting:

```yaml
model_config:
  output_dir: "{{ project('named_paths').sql_output_dir }}"
  source_model: "{{ model('id') }}"
  mappings:
    source_table: '{{ ref("source_model", "customers") }}'
```

`this()` reads from the current configuration object, `project()` reads from
the project configuration, `model()` reads from the active model, and `scope()`
looks up a parent value. `ref("model_id", "object_id")` resolves an object in
a named model, and dot notation can read a field from that object. Expressions
can also produce native YAML values, including lists.

#### 2.2 Include Shared Configuration

Use `include` when a project or model should load configuration from one or
more separate YAML files. Ordinary include paths are resolved from the project
root, and included values become part of the configuration being built:

```yaml
# ramona.yaml
include:
  - ./config/shared_objects.yml
  - ./config/generation_defaults.yml

id: warehouse
models_dir: ./models/
templates_dir: ./templates/
generated_paths:
  - ./sql/
```

##### 2.3 Include
An included model configuration can provide shared settings to several model
definitions:

```yaml
# models/raw/model_config.yaml
include:
  - config/raw_defaults.yaml

model_config:
  id: raw
  schema: RAW
```

The DuckDB example uses this pattern in
[ramona.yaml](sample_projects/duck_db_dwh/ramona.yaml) and its
[project configuration includes](sample_projects/duck_db_dwh/90_models/includes/project_configs).

#### 2.4 Extend a Base Object

Use `extends` when objects share a base definition. The child object names the
base YAML file, then overrides or adds its own values:

```yaml
# models/warehouse/tables.yml
objects:
  - extends: ./models/base/raw_table.yaml
    id: customers
    table_name: customers
    description: Customer records
    columns:
      - id: customer_id
        datatype: INTEGER
```

A base file can hold reusable generation settings:

```yaml
# models/base/raw_table.yaml
include:
  - ./table_defaults.yaml

database: RAW
```

This lets each child object inherit common settings while retaining a small,
readable object definition. The DuckDB sample applies `extends` to its raw
table objects in [bronze_tables.yml](sample_projects/duck_db_dwh/90_models/knmi_model/bronze_tables.yml)
and keeps the shared definition in
[raw_table.yaml](sample_projects/duck_db_dwh/90_models/extends/tables/raw_table.yaml).


### 3. Generate
you can generate in two ways

#### 3.1 generate tamples
Place a Jinja2 template below `templates_dir`. Ramona passes the current object
to the template and derives the output extension from the template filename:

```jinja2
-- templates/table.sql.jinja2
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {{ object.name or object.id }} (
{% for column in object.columns %}
		{{ column.name or column.id }} {{ column.datatype }}{% if not loop.last %},{% endif %}
{% endfor %}
);
```

With the configuration above, `generate` writes a SQL file below the model's
`output_dir`. Set `append: true` in a template configuration when multiple
objects should append to the same output file.

the generator passes the following context:
- Object: The object to be generated

##### 3.1.1 Append

Set `append: true` in a template configuration when multiple
objects should append to the same output file.

example

When appending you get also a varaible to check if this is the first append.


### 3.2 Copy Existing Files

Generation can copy a file or every item in a directory instead of rendering a
template:

```yaml
objects:
  - id: seed_database
    template_config:
      - copy_from: ./assets/create_database.sql
        output_dir: ./sql/
```


### 4. Validate

From the repository root, run the development sample:

```powershell
ramona -rcp .\sample_projects\project_for_development\ramona.yaml modelcheck
```

Use `generate` after changing models or templates. Use `modelcheck` to run the
Python checks in the configured `modelchecks_dir`; checks report passed,
failed, warning, and skipped results in the console. Generated directories are
cleaned at the start of generation, so keep generated paths separate from
hand-maintained files.



The `copy_from` path must exist when generation runs. See the development sample
for both file and directory copy configurations.



##### 4.1 Model Checks

Checks receive a model object and return a `CheckResult`:

```python
from ramona.modelcheck import CheckResult, modelcheck


@modelcheck(name="Has columns", description="Tables must define columns")
def check_columns(model):
    if "columns" in model:
        return CheckResult.success()
    return CheckResult.failure("All tables require a columns key.")
```

The public model-checking API also exports `ModelCheckConfig` for setting
severity and conditions. See the working examples in
[modelchecks_all.py](sample_projects/project_for_development/modelchecks/modelchecks_all.py)
and [modelchecks_tables.py](sample_projects/project_for_development/modelchecks/modelchecks_tables.py).

## Examples

The [development sample](sample_projects/project_for_development) exercises
model discovery, nested YAML objects, template rendering, copying files and
directories, references, and model checks:

```powershell
ramona -rcp .\sample_projects\project_for_development\ramona.yaml generate
ramona -rcp .\sample_projects\project_for_development\ramona.yaml modelcheck
```

The [DuckDB data-warehouse sample](sample_projects/duck_db_dwh) demonstrates a
larger workflow with raw and platform SQL, orchestration files, configuration
includes, and inherited model definitions. Its own
[sample README](sample_projects/duck_db_dwh/readme.md) documents the sample-specific
KNMI API key prerequisite; Ramona itself does not require that key.



The main runtime areas are generation, YAML/Jinja2 resolution, reference
resolution, and model checking. Detailed API documentation is not currently
published; the source and samples are the authoritative references.

## Getting Help

For questions, bug reports, or feature requests, use the repository's
[GitHub Issues](https://github.com/ozcanseker/Ramona/issues). Include your
Python version, Ramona command, a minimal configuration example, and relevant
output from `log/ramona.log`.
